# PicoCalc-SD-Drive

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

Author: Thomas Dzubin    Version: V0.01A (set in [PicoCalc-SD-Drive.h](PicoCalc-SD-Drive.h))

Plug a ClockworkPi PicoCalc into a PC with a USB cable and it shows up as a **USB
drive**, using the **SD card in the PicoCalc** as the disc. Copy files to and from
the card from the PC, without taking the card out.

The PicoCalc's screen shows what the drive is doing, and two keys on the PicoCalc
control it.

## What it does

- The PC sees an ordinary removable USB drive (USB mass storage). The PC handles the
  file system on the card (FAT, exFAT or anything else); the PicoCalc only moves
  512 byte blocks.
- While plugged in, the **PC owns the card**: the PicoCalc does not use the card
  itself, because a drive cannot safely be shared.
- The drive stays visible when the card is removed and reports "no media", like a
  real card reader, and recovers when a card is put in.

## Speed: this drive is SLOW

**Expect roughly 0.3 to 0.6 MB/s, about 100 times slower than the same SD card in a
card reader on the PC.** Read this before you plan to copy anything big.

Measured with this program (200 files from 0 bytes to 4 MB, 84.7 MB in all, read back from
the card itself, not from the Windows cache):

| | RP2350 PicoCalc | RP2040 PicoCalc |
|---|---|---|
| PC writing to the drive | about 0.37 MB/s | about 0.27 MB/s |
| PC reading from the drive | about 0.57 MB/s | about 0.52 MB/s |

On the RP2350 the card itself managed about 2.0 MB/s reading and 1.0 MB/s writing (the
PicoCalc screen shows the card speed of the last copy). The PC sees less than that because
of USB command overhead and the way Windows writes, and because many small files cost more
than one big one.

For comparison, the same card in a Windows machine typically does about 60 to 95 MB/s
reading and 20 to 60 MB/s writing in a USB 3 reader or a good built-in slot, and about 20 to
35 MB/s in a cheap USB 2 reader. Those are typical figures, not measured here, and they
depend on the card and the reader.

What that means in practice:

| Amount | Read at about 0.57 MB/s | Write at about 0.37 MB/s | Card in a fast PC reader |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 MB | 2 seconds | 3 seconds | under a second |
| 100 MB | 3 minutes | 4.5 minutes | a few seconds |
| 1 GB | 30 minutes | 45 minutes | about 15 seconds |
| the whole 29.5 GB card | about 15 hours | about 23 hours | about 5 to 25 minutes |

This is good for moving programs, screenshots, documents and other small files on and off
the card without taking it out. For bulk copying, take the card out and use a card reader.

Why it is slow:

1. **USB full speed.** The RP2040 and RP2350 only do USB at 12 Mbit/s, which in practice
   tops out at about 1 MB/s. That alone is 30 to 80 times slower than a USB 3 card reader,
   and nothing in the firmware can change it.
2. **SPI mode.** The PicoCalc talks to the card over a single data line at 25 MHz, which is at
   most about 3 MB/s (about 2 MB/s measured). A PC reader uses the 4 bit SD bus, typically at
   least 10 times faster, and the faster UHS modes besides.
3. **Small transfers.** Each USB transfer is 2 KB (four blocks, see `CFG_TUD_MSC_EP_BUFSIZE`
   in `tusb_config.h`). A bigger buffer might gain a little, but the USB limit still applies,
   so the most that could be gained from software is roughly a factor of two.
4. **A busy card.** A write has to wait for the card to finish programming its flash, which
   the SD specification allows to take a quarter of a second per block; cards vary a lot.

## The PicoCalc screen and keys

The screen shows: whether the PC is connected, the card (size and type, or "none"
/ "cannot be read"), the drive state (ready, ejected, no media), whether writes are
allowed, how much has been read and written, any errors, and a live READING /
WRITING indicator.

| Key | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **E** | Eject the drive (the PC sees the disc removed), press again to mount it again |
| **W** | Turn write protection on or off (the PC is told the drive is write protected, and refuses writes) |
| **~** (Shift + backtick) | Reboot to BOOTSEL mode, to flash a new `.uf2` |

Ejecting from the PC (the usual "Safely remove" or "Eject") also marks the drive as
ejected; press **E** on the PicoCalc to mount it again.

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with `PICO_SDK_PATH` set.
Pick the board with `-DPICO_BOARD=pico` (RP2040) or `-DPICO_BOARD=pico2` (RP2350):

    cmake -B build-rp2350 -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2
    ninja -C build-rp2350

Output: `PicoCalc-SD-Drive-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2040` or `RP2350`), also copied
to the top-level folder. Flash it by copying it to the `RPI-RP2` / `RP2350` drive: hold
BOOTSEL on power-up, or press `~` (Shift + backtick) on the PicoCalc while this
firmware is running.

## Files

The program is one source file and one header:

| File | What it is |
|------|------------|
| `PicoCalc-SD-Drive.c` | **The whole program.** `main()` is at the top, followed by six labelled sections that build on each other: 1. SD card blocks (our own reads and writes with the SD specification's busy waits, instead of the starter's block routines, which stop waiting for a busy card after a few milliseconds and then fail for ever), 2. the media (the card: insert and remove, its size, retries and recovery), 3. drive state (ejected, write protect, counters, speed), 4. USB descriptors, 5. USB mass storage (answers the PC's requests), 6. the status screen |
| `PicoCalc-SD-Drive.h` | **Every constant, setting and shared type**, in numbered sections, including the version number (`SD_DRIVE_VERSION`) |
| `tusb_config.h` | TinyUSB's settings file. It has to have exactly this name, so it is the one extra file |
| `CMakeLists.txt`, `pico_sdk_import.cmake` | The build |
| `stresstest.ps1`, `stressverify.ps1` | Windows PowerShell stress test, see Testing below |
| `LICENSE` | MIT |
| `picocalc-text-starter-main/` | Vendored picocalc-text-starter by Blair Leduc (SD card start-up, LCD, fonts, keyboard, south bridge drivers). Read-only |

In the single file the SD card, USB and screen code are separate sections, but nothing but
discipline keeps them apart: only section 1 and 2 should touch the card, and only section 6
the LCD.

## Notes

- Speed is covered in its own section above: it is slow, and that cannot be fixed in software.
  The screen shows the card speed of the last copy.
- The screen also shows the card's raw size register (CSD) and whether it was read twice
  with a matching checksum. If a size ever looks wrong, the hex string there says what the
  card reported.
- If a card gets stuck after errors (the screen says "cannot be read"), take the card out
  and put it back in; the drive then recovers by itself.
- There is no Format key on the PicoCalc, on purpose: the PC owns the file system. To format the
  card, plug the PicoCalc in and format the drive from the PC (in Windows: right-click the drive,
  Format, or `format D: /fs:fat32 /q` with your drive letter). Formatting erases everything on the card.
- The drive is only as safe as any USB drive: eject it from the PC before unplugging, and
  do not pull the card while the PC is writing.

## Testing

Two PowerShell scripts check that the drive stores data correctly. Set `$drive` at the top
of each to the drive letter Windows gave the PicoCalc (they write only to a new `sdtest2`
folder on the card, and delete nothing).

1. `stresstest.ps1` writes 200 files of mixed sizes (0 bytes to 4 MB, 84.7 MB in all) from
   known random data, flushes the Windows cache and reads them back. This alone proves only
   that the writes were accepted, because Windows serves the read-back from its own cache.
2. Press **E** twice on the PicoCalc (eject, mount again) so Windows forgets what it cached,
   then run `stressverify.ps1`. It rebuilds the expected data from the same seeds and
   compares checksums, so the data really comes from the SD card.

Each prints a PASS or FAIL line into a `.log` file next to the script. To test pulling the
card, copy a large file to the drive and take the card out part way: the copy should fail
with "device is not ready", and the drive should be back, with the card's other files intact,
once the card is put back in. Delete `sdtest2` from the card when you are done.

MIT, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). The vendored `picocalc-text-starter-main/` is Blair Leduc's

## Status

Version V0.01A, built and tested on both the RP2350 and the RP2040 PicoCalc (2026-09-30 to 2026-10-01). The PC sees a USB drive with the right card size, files copy both ways, and eject, write protect and card removal work.

Stress test, run on both chips with the final code (including the code review fixes in the CHANGELOG): 200 files from 0 bytes to 4 MB (84.7 MB), written, then read back after pressing E twice so Windows read them from the card and not from its cache. Every file matched its SHA-256 checksum and the PicoCalc showed 0 errors. Card to PC speed was about 0.57 MB/s on the RP2350 and 0.52 MB/s on the RP2040; writing took 219 s and 309 s.

Pulling the card in the middle of a 32 MB copy, on both chips, gave a clean "device is not ready" on the PC with no hang, and the drive came back when the card was put back in (the PicoCalc counted 2 errors on the RP2350 and 1 on the RP2040, for the transfers in flight at that moment, and no more). The file that was being copied held exactly the data written before the pull, and every other file was still intact. Windows marks the volume "Warning" (dirty) after that, and `chkdsk /f` clears it.
